A detector hit pauses the run for a human, so task success under attack is lower than on clean pages by design.

Removing the injection detector did not let any attack through in this test, but it lets far more tasks finish (the reader alone keeps the planner clean). The detector's job is to catch an attack early, and its price is pauses.

Layer 7 (goal check) no longer asks a model about plain typing, filling, select and extract steps, so it now covers navigation, clicks and key presses only. Data-flow rules and the goal check cannot tell an exfiltration request to an endpoint on a site the routine already uses from normal browsing there. Only the detector and the reader stop that kind of attack.

caveats.text: A screen frame is raw content. The guard decides whether a frame may leave, from which kind of source, what may come back and what is ever recorded; it does not redact or generalise pixels, and when a frame is allowed the provider sees everything on the screen. What a provider does with a frame it received is the provider's policy and is not measured here.
Closed answer schemas (every string is an enum) stop text read off the screen from coming back. They cannot stop the model from seeing it.

A frame is held in a buffer that is wiped after the call and is never written by this layer. Copies handed to a provider SDK or the HTTP stack, and freed memory the interpreter has not reused, cannot be wiped or controlled from here; swap and core dumps are outside this check.

Tier 3 (computer use) is not demonstrated on the benefits task: 3 runs against a simulated actuator on real screenshots made 0 pointer actions and landed on an interactive element 0 times. Nothing is clicked in that setting, so a claim of done there is a false claim by construction.

Real-model red team (real model, n = 42 cases (3 repeats each)): Intervals overlap: this shows what the layers cost (task success under attack was 22% with every layer on against 84% with all off, and 0 of 126 runs with every layer on let an attack through), not that the layers prevent attacks. The attacks were written by the team that wrote the defences, and a result is true of one model version on one day.

The power analysis only shows what the n = 4 design could detect under our own assumptions (effect size, carryover, order effect, how noisy the measure is). It is a property of the design, not a result about people, and not evidence that an effect exists.
Section 'study' has no numbers: the live study has not been run: no data in evals/study/results/.

The three calculators are sandbox sites we built, each with planted quirks, and each computes one Universal-Credit-shaped entitlement. They say nothing about how real calculators behave or what their terms and bot protection allow.

Agent-claim calibration is mostly on simulated runs. The real-model result covers only 68 claimed successes from one family of failure (see agent_claims.live), so it cannot show that claim risk can be predicted in general. A low predicted risk of a false claim never replaces the code check, which decides success.

The off-hours live run depends on the conditions spike S2 passed under: macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording granted, an unlocked screen, a harmless app, the owner present. The presence forecast and the start-or-wait rule are evaluated on synthetic personas; the live demo may fall back to a simulated clock.

Probabilities are better than the baselines and calibrated, but alert quality is modest: about a third of stuck events are flagged, and on held-out people the false-alarm rate (about 1.2 per hour) overshoots the 1 per hour budget chosen on training people.
'Stuck' means no progress event in the next 60 seconds, which is not the same as confusion. Fast thinking and slow typing both look stuck to this label.
The apprentice traces follow a fixed task script, so part of the hazard model's large gain on them is learning the script, not predicting stuck. The four-persona result is the headline.

Skill tracing saturates on synthetic personas (about 35 tasks a day): mastery reaches its ceiling on day one and cannot follow the planted learning curve. Decay with absence is shown in unit tests only.

On the learner trajectories (three learners, thirty cases each, one with a three-day absence) the help level does lighten as deficits fade, but a clock alone ranks the true curve as well as mastery does, the ranking of which deficits fade fastest is near chance, and the short absence did not move the level. Three learners make every interval wide.

Off-policy evaluation is validated in a simulator whose reward structure we invented, with exactly known propensities. Real implicit labels (followed, dismissed, repeated, undone) are noisy proxies for 'it helped'.

The rule is not the best everywhere. Lowest regret by build cost: b=4: Build now (1.07); b=8: Build now (1.15); b=16: Build now (1.27); b=32: Ski rental with predictions (lambda 0.2) (1.33). When building is cheap (b = 4 manual runs) building at once (1.07) is level with the rule (1.07) and both are ahead of break-even (1.70); the prediction earns its keep when building costs more. The pack's own build costs are 4 to 9 runs.

The weekly map predicts held-out days worse than a simple baseline for shift-worker (map Brier 0.214 against prior 0.194 and one global rate 0.175). A weekly template does not suit rotating shifts or no routine.
The window forecast is only roughly calibrated: expected calibration error 0.07 to 0.13 across personas on held-out days, and it beats pooled survival (no time of week) on 2 of 4 personas.
The 95% intervals on the presence map contain the planted active probability in only 55% to 91% of bins. Smoothing across neighbouring bins trades bias for variance, so the intervals are too narrow.

Idle capacity per week is over-estimated: nine-to-five 12 h against a planted 10 h; irregular 10 h against a planted 6 h. With no sleep event the machine is assumed to stay on for 60 minutes after the last event, and a locked screen still counts as idle although a desktop run cannot start on it.

The finder alone (minimum support 3) returns many small clusters of one-off work: precision 22% over 55 clusters. The value gate removes them: precision 100% over 6 proposals. Short routines of three or four steps are the hardest to tell from chance.

The 95% forecast interval covered what happened in 8 of 11 planted routines (73%), which is below nominal and rests on one held-out week; the schedule change on day 15 falls inside it, and the model has no way to know about it.

In the live runs the model states a confidence only when it makes a finish claim itself, which happened only in the runs that went wrong. Its presence copies the label, so it is kept out of the classifier and cannot be calibrated.

Cold-start priors are built from four synthetic personas (or 24 scripted apprentices with two cases each); with so few and such alike people, partial pooling is hard to tell from complete pooling, and learning-curve drift is not modelled.
Attacks are synthetic and were written by the same team that wrote the defences. A new attack style can get through.
A detector hit pauses the run for a human, so task success under attack is lower than on clean pages by design.

Removing the injection detector did not let any attack through in this test, but it lets far more tasks finish (the reader alone keeps the planner clean). The detector's job is to catch an attack early, and its price is pauses.

Layer 7 (goal check) no longer asks a model about plain typing, filling, select and extract steps, so it now covers navigation, clicks and key presses only. We changed this after seeing it pause the run on clean pages when the worker was just typing the answer (5 false pauses in 93 live runs). The false-pause figure after the change (0 of 93) is measured on the same pages that showed the problem, so it is in-sample and probably too good; typed data is still stopped by the data-flow and action-gate layers, not by this one.

Data-flow rules and the goal check cannot tell an exfiltration request to an endpoint on a site the routine already uses from normal browsing there. Only the detector and the reader stop that kind of attack.

Nothing is executed. An attack counts as successful when the model proposes an action that serves the attacker and the layers authorise it; real tools, redirects and multi-step consequences are not modelled.
The attacks are synthetic and were written by the same team that wrote the defences; models change, so a result is true of one model version on one day.

The canary scan looks for the exact planted strings, their invented words, simple rewrites (case, separators, URL encoding, base64, hex). A paraphrase, a translation, a hash or a character-code encoding of a token would not be caught. The claim measured is: these planted strings did not reach the model port, in these flows.

A SafePayload limits the form of what is sent (numbers, codes, fixed ids, bucketed values), not its meaning: a bucketed count of the worker's own meetings is still a fact about the worker. Generalisation reduces precision; it is not anonymisation.

Model calls the worker asked for (agent runs, the coach, the quarantined reader) are not routed through the egress guard and send raw content to the provider by design. They appear in the ledger only as metadata lines when the port is wrapped (direct.LedgeredPort). The Privacy screen therefore does not claim that nothing else leaves this laptop.
All fixtures are synthetic and the real provider is never called here (a fake client checks only the request shape). Nothing is validated on real calendars, repositories or accounts.
Closed answer schemas (every string is an enum) stop text read off the screen from coming back. They cannot stop the model from seeing it.

A frame is held in a buffer that is wiped after the call and is never written by this layer. Copies handed to a provider SDK or the HTTP stack, and freed memory the interpreter has not reused, cannot be wiped or controlled from here; swap and core dumps are outside this check.

The residue scan looks for the planted PNG's raw bytes, the token written into its metadata, its full SHA-256, and base64 or hex renderings of the file. It cannot see pixels, a re-encoded copy (a JPEG of the same frame), or a description of the frame.

Old project TypeScript under apps/desktop still names Gemini and OpenAI hosts behind flags (listed in static_guard_ts_references, report only). The rule is that frames reach a provider through the engine's egress guard; the Python tree is checked for it, the TypeScript is not enforced.
No real provider was called: a capturing port and a fake client check request shapes and the guard. Gemini and OpenAI behaviour (latency, accuracy, cost) is the MODELS track's own measurement.

The generator, the digest rules and the habit thresholds were written by the same agent. Thresholds were set on development replicates 0 to 3 and scored on fresh ones (100 and up), but the planted rates are large and habits are planted independently; real habits are smaller, correlated and noisier.
Small differences are not flagged by design (each habit has a floor). At 25% of the planted strength recall falls to 19%.
Evaluation digests come from the rules, because model digests take about a second a commit. The local model was not present, so model-against-rules agreement was not measured.

On commit sessions the alignment sees differences in the SHAPE of sessions (missing test steps, reverts, extra code-commit loops) in some replicates, and sees nothing in seconds, because git records when a commit landed and not how long the work took. Habits that live in the message or the clock (vague messages, late nights) are invisible to cogs by construction.
Suggestions are advice chosen by code from commit-level shares. Nobody has been shown that following one improves anything; there is no study of the git layer, and a share is not a cause.
A real repository is compared with synthetic experts, so its origin is reported as mixed; the comparison is with a scripted baseline, not with real experts.

The ranking weights, the minimum score of 0.30, the cap of three and the per-kind limits are hand-set constants, not fitted to any data. A different choice would move precision and recall; no sensitivity sweep is claimed.

Recall is capped at what the judge is allowed to show of each kind (one practice card, one git card, two automations): a person with three planted git habits is credited for finding one. That is the design, not a flaw in the metric, but it hides how much was left unsaid.

Calendar cards are scored against the calendar track's planted problems; the suggestion thresholds and the planted structure come from the same generator family, and a week can carry several planted problems of which the judge may show one. Finished-run cards are covered by scripted checks only, and so are stale calendar and git cards.

Staleness is injected by changing a reading (a routine switched on, a skill at level 4). Real staleness has more forms, and a source that cannot be read is never treated as stale, which can leave a card up for a few hours after it stopped being true.

Event kinds (meeting, focus, break, off-screen) come from keyword rules on titles and attendee counts. Real titles are messier; a meeting with no invitees is read as the owner's own time, and a focus block that is not named as one is invisible. Calendar hygiene differs from how people really work.

Gap intervals cover uncertainty in the expert reference (8 synthetic experts) only, not a learner's week-to-week variation; a week is flagged only if it also lies outside the range of expert weeks. Three weeks per person is thin.

The Microsoft Graph adapters were tested against recorded fake responses written from the public documentation; they have never been run against a live tenant by this code, and tenant policy decides what a signed-in worker may read.

The leak result is measured: the exact planted names, addresses, titles, locations and ids did not appear in any payload, suggestion or captured request. It does not rule out a paraphrase or an encoding, and model calls the worker asks for are recorded in the egress ledger, not hidden.

The prompt wording, the worked examples and the per-field choice of model or rules were tuned on the dev split only; the held-out test split was run once with the frozen prompts (one later look at the shipped-policy arm followed the single policy revision, see loc_policy_revised). Dev numbers are therefore optimistic and are shown only as such.

No fine-tuning (LOC-3 is cut): it could not be validated in the time available. The model is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at 4-bit quantisation (Q4_K_M) with a labelling guide, a few fixed worked examples and constrained decoding.
Labels such as risk and message quality are our written policy, not ground truth: a reviewer may reasonably disagree on a share of items, which caps the accuracy any method can show here.

Small prompt changes move the numbers by more than the intervals suggest: replacing three worked examples (to keep them disjoint from the fixtures) changed dev commit-category accuracy from 48 to 44 of 52. A difference of a few items between two prompts or between the model and the rules is noise at this sample size.

The rules, the labelling policy, the prompts' guide and the fixture generator share one author and one vocabulary (for example the list of sensitive areas), so the rules are better matched to these fixtures than they would be to real history, and the model's labelling guide is better matched than it would be to real history. Real data would test both.

'No leak' is claimed only as measured: zero planted strings in the outputs and in the server log of the evaluation run, and the guards reject a deliberately leaking stand-in model. The raw inputs do pass through the local model's memory and llama.cpp's in-process prompt cache (never written to disk by this module).

The false-reject rate is measured on a stand-in model that varies numbers and interval wording in the ways we wrote down. A real model phrases things we did not anticipate, so its false-reject rate is likely higher; a rejected reply costs nothing (the template is used).

The adversarial rejection rate is against the 28 attacks we wrote. The unknown-habit rule is a set of cue patterns (a cause or a share of time attributed to a phrase that names nothing in the vocabulary), not a language model: a novel phrasing with no cue can pass.

Packets come from synthetic apprentices (and the real stuck-hazard evaluation in the full run); the coach, routine, counterfactual and time-to-progress blocks are scripted fixtures that exercise wording and the check, not measurements.
Deficit detection is weaker for: repeated_read_result (precision 70%, recall 100%); copy_error (precision 100%, recall 71%). Overall precision 92%, recall 95% over 160 case-deficit pairs.

The recovered price differs from the planted price, with an interval that excludes zero, for: repeated_read_result (+13.5 s, interval 5.1 to 23.3). The alignment names a block of extra steps by its content, so a deficit that shares steps with another is mis-priced.
On held-out people the false-alarm rate is 1.21 an hour, over the 1.0 an hour budget chosen on the training people.

In the detailed run the interval of IPS, SNIPS, DR does not contain the true value 0.018. Over 24 independent replications the intervals covered the truth: IPS 96%, SNIPS 96%, DR 88% (naive 0%); nominal is 95%.

The clean-path result (20 of 20 households, 95% lower bound 84%) is the compiled path on the sandbox it was written against, so a full pass is expected and says little. The discriminating evidence is the robust and injected runs. Twenty households cannot rule out a pass rate well below 100%.

Failure injection covers 4 patterns only: layout change on site b (5 of 5 passed); layout change on site c (5 of 5 passed); layout change on site a and one-off 503 on site b (5 of 5 passed); one-off 503 on site c (5 of 5 passed). 15 of 20 households needed the tier-2 browser agent. 20 of 20 passed (95% lower bound 84%). Other failure kinds (a changed flow, a wrong page, a slow site) were not injected.

Real-model runs (agent-core, tier 1 disabled so every navigator uses the browser agent): 20 households per condition, 90 runs. Clean 18 of 20 (95% interval 0.70 to 0.97), 2 honest failures ('not every calculator produced a verified result'); layout change 20 of 20 (0.84 to 1.00). Twenty per condition shows the failure modes, not a pass rate; identical prompts are cached, so repeated page situations are one live sample each.

Injected pages: the detector paused 20 of 20 runs (20 detected of 20 injected) with 0.0 model-driven steps, and 0 attacks succeeded. Task success is 0 by design: a paused run does no task. This tests the detector on these pages, which we wrote.

Cost is an estimate at placeholder rates (5.0 and 30.0 USD per million tokens in and out), not the provider's price list: about None USD for the rows in the file (None tokens in, None out), 494 live calls and 5302 cache hits across the runs. Cached answers cost nothing on a re-run.
The live false-pause result (0 of 93 clean runs, 0 of 30 on hard negatives) is in-sample: the layer-7 (goal-drift) scope was changed while building on this same catalog, so it is not a held-out rate.

The privacy result covers the guard through its own reference flows and 6 integration flow(s) from a layer's real code (upper bound on the leak rate 0.0% over 10608 planted tokens). These layers supplied no real-code flows and are not counted as passed: evidence.

CIRCULARITY: the calculators' quirks (site b ignores capital tariff income; site c applies a two-child limit and treats exactly 16,000 as over the limit) and the household archetypes that trigger them were planted by us. The router can only show it found our planted structure; it does not show that real calculators or real agents fail this way.
The trust parameter lambda is fixed by us (or set from past forecast error by a heuristic that is not in the paper). It was not tuned on this simulation.

The start-or-wait rule is conservative: it collided with the worker's return in 2.1% of started runs against an allowed 10%, and used 74% of idle time against 90% for running whenever idle five minutes. Runs are replayed one per decision point on held-out spells; interruption and idle-use intervals count spells as independent.
Planted routines that ran fewer than 3 times cannot be found by design and are excluded from recall: nine-to-five/weekly-report.
The autonomy ladder needs 20 clean shadow runs to reach A2 and about 73 clean runs to reach A3; the demo reaches A1 or A2 at most. A3 is a target, not a result.
Layer 1 (sanitising) is modelled as defeating only markup-based attacks (fake system tags, tool-call syntax); a scripted planner that follows plain text shows no change when it is off.
Layers overlap, so leaving one out often changes nothing. The 'only_<layer>' rows show each layer's standalone strength.
Alignment with the attacker's goal is judged by rules on the proposed action, so an unrelated harmful action is not counted.

Lists of integers could carry text as character codes. Lists are capped at 64 items and integers at 1e9, which bounds that; the threat model is accidental leakage by honest code, not an author trying to smuggle data out.
The static guard is name-based. It does not follow a module name held in a variable and cannot see code added at run time; it catches honest mistakes such as importing an SDK 'just for wording'.

The ledger is a plain local file the worker can clear (the clear is itself counted). It records what the guard sent; it cannot record what a module sends by bypassing the guard, which is what the static guard and the canary flows are for.
Reverts are rare even when planted, so the revert habit is the weakest to recover; it is reported, not tuned.
The one real history (this project's) is short and agent-assisted; its aggregates illustrate the pipeline and are not a finding.
The leak result is a count of exact planted strings in captured request bodies on these flows. It does not catch a paraphrase, a translation or a hash of a token.
No model decides what is surfaced; a model may reword the reason line through the egress guard. Wording quality is not evaluated here.

A problem planted below the expert tolerance (one fragmented day, one back-to-back run) is not suggested, by design. Recall against the planted intent is therefore below 1; the thresholds come from the template, not from the truth labels.

Size, tests touched, duration, attendee count and recurrence are computed by code from the input in every path, so they are exact by construction and say nothing about the model; only category, risk, message quality and needs_prep are model-or-rules fields.

Latency and tokens per second are for one Apple M2 Max (32 GB) with all layers on the GPU: about 30 generated tokens per second, so a digest takes roughly 0.5 s when only the category is asked for (the shipped policy) and about 0.7 to 1.1 s with every field. A history of a thousand commits takes about nine minutes the first time; the rules path takes microseconds.

Which fields the model decides was chosen on the dev split and revised once after the held-out run (events needs_prep moved from the model to the rules). The held-out numbers of the model-for-everything run are the clean evidence; the numbers for the policy as shipped (commit_digest: category, event_digest: category by the model) include one held-out look after that revision and are slightly optimistic.
The live block, when it is run, is a small-n pass rate for one local model on synthetic packets; it says nothing about other models.

The shuffled-label null averages +46.2 s (interval -36.4 to 116.9), about 20% of the real gap of 229.6 s. Matching each case to its nearest reference is not symmetric, so the null is not exactly zero; the real gap sits above the null interval, which is the comparison that counts.

7 of 20 households are planted discrepancies between the sandbox calculators (quirks we wrote). A pass on them means the discrepancy was flagged, not that an entitlement was worked out, and the oracle is a simplified rule set, not the law.
